title: Faith as faithfulness
hook: faith is also showing up, again and again
tomorrow: Year four close: the many rooms

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith as trust: a storm, a sleeping teacher, and the question, where is your faith? Your line was faith is trust. Who did you let take a little of your weight? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

An open window, facing Jerusalem. A new law has just been signed: for thirty days, anyone who prays to any god or man except the king goes to the lions. Daniel knows it's signed. He goes home, up to his room, where the windows are open toward Jerusalem. And the Book of Daniel says he "kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." As he did aforetime. Nothing new. No speech, no protest. He just keeps doing what he did before, at the window, in plain sight. Today's word: faith as faithfulness.
screen: `A LAW SIGNED: PRAY TO NO ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's Greek word, pistis, meant trust. It also means faithfulness: keeping faith, the way you keep a promise or keep showing up for a friend. You can see both in one verse. When Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit, the King James Bible reads: "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith." Faith, on a list of ways a person acts, right beside gentleness and goodness. Here it reads like faithfulness: something you keep doing. Trust is leaning your weight on someone. Faithfulness is coming back, again and again, whether or not you feel it that day. And one old song puts God's faithfulness before ours. The Book of Lamentations is a book of grief, sung over a city in ruins. This path heard the line a few weeks ago; this time, listen for its last word: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." New every morning. Faithfulness, in that line, isn't a feeling. It's what shows up the next day, and the next. The second letter to Timothy has a line for days when people's faith gives out: "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself." After these weeks of grief and doubt, that line has a job. On a day when you can't feel trust at all, you can still be faithful. You can come back to the window. Daniel's prayer at the window wasn't proof that he felt brave. It was what he did aforetime, done once more.

Here's the practice: show up again. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you used to do faithfully and have let slip. A call to someone. A walk. A prayer. A page of reading. A promise you made to yourself. Don't scold yourself for letting it go. Just look at it, the way Daniel looked at his open window. Then choose one small way to come back to it today, smaller than you think it needs to be. If you pray, you can say: great is thy faithfulness. If you don't, simply notice that you showed up here, today. The bell holds the time.
Faith as faithfulness. Pistis as keeping faith: coming back again and again, like Daniel at his window, held up by a faithfulness that is new every morning.
Your line: keep showing up. Do the small thing you chose, once, today. Not perfectly. Just as you did aforetime. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Some Christians practice faithfulness through regular habits: daily prayer at set times, weekly worship, and keeping promises such as marriage vows and baptismal vows, including through seasons when faith feels dry.

original.note: Greek: faith, and also faithfulness. in the King James list of the fruit of the Spirit it is translated faith.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means feeling sure.
what it means: faith is also faithfulness: showing up again, like Daniel at his window, whether you feel it or not.
what a scholar hears: the King James has faith in the fruit of the Spirit, on a list of ways a person acts, and the Greek word there is pistis, the same word as yesterday's trust.

notes: Daniel 6:7 gives the decree as thirty days, covering petitions to 'any God or man' except the king; the hook paraphrases. Confirm.
2 Timothy: the script says 'Paul, or one of his followers' to reflect differing views on authorship. Keeper may prefer 'Paul's second letter to Timothy' without comment.
'Some newer translations give that word as faithfulness' (Galatians 5:22) is a translation claim; confirm phrasing.
Lamentations described as 'a book of grief, sung over a city in ruins', from its content; no author or date is given.
howItsDone mentions marriage and baptismal vows; confirm.
